kcet|Chemistry|2017|32||0|0.s:
Physical adsorption is held together only by weak van der Waals forces, and it is exothermic.
Apply Le Chatelier to the equilibrium gas ⇌ adsorbed gas + heat.
(D) Low temperature — the forward step gives out heat, so cooling drives it forward ✓ favourable.
(B) High pressure — adsorption reduces the number of free gas molecules, so raising the pressure
drives it forward ✓ favourable.
(C) A higher critical temperature means the gas is more easily liquefied, which is the same thing
as saying its molecules attract each other more strongly, so it is adsorbed more readily ✓ favourable.
(A) High temperature — heating supplies the small enthalpy of adsorption (20–40 kJ mol⁻¹) back
to the molecules, and they simply desorb. This is the one condition that works against it.
∴ high temperature is not favourable.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|33||0|0:
This is leaching, a chemical separation used when the ore is very dilute.
Silver (and gold) are extracted by the Mac Arthur–Forrest cyanide process.
The crushed ore is treated with dilute NaCN in the presence of air; the metal dissolves as a
soluble complex:
4Ag + 8CN⁻ + 2H₂O + O₂ ⇒ 4[Ag(CN)₂]⁻ + 4OH⁻
Air is essential — it is the oxidising agent that takes Ag to Ag⁺.
The silver is then displaced from the solution by a more reactive metal, zinc:
2[Ag(CN)₂]⁻ + Zn ⇒ [Zn(CN)₄]²⁻ + 2Ag
Aluminium is leached with NaOH (Bayer process), not cyanide; copper is usually roasted and
smelted; sodium is obtained by electrolysis of fused NaCl.
∴ silver.
kcet|Chemistry|2017|34||0|0:
Brine is aqueous NaCl, so the chlorine is present as chloride ion, Cl⁻, at oxidation state −1.
The chlorine we want, Cl₂, is at oxidation state 0.
Going from −1 to 0 is a loss of electrons, which is oxidation:
2Cl⁻ ⇒ Cl₂ + 2e⁻
Industrially this is done at the anode during the electrolysis of brine, where the anode is simply
the electrode that takes those electrons away.
It cannot be reduction (C) — that would drive chloride to a still lower state, which does not exist.
Chlorination (B) means adding chlorine to something else, and acidification (D) is irrelevant here.
∴ it is based on oxidation.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|35||0|0.s:
A pπ–pπ bond needs two p orbitals to overlap sideways, and that only works if the atoms are
small enough to come close together.
Nitrogen is a second period element with no d orbitals and a small atomic radius, so its 2p
orbitals overlap sideways effectively. Two nitrogens form one σ and two π bonds: N≡N.
Phosphorus, selenium and tellurium are all larger. Their 3p, 4p and 5p orbitals are more diffuse
and the nuclei cannot approach closely enough for good sideways overlap.
Those elements get round it by forming more single bonds instead — which is why phosphorus
exists as P₄ with six P–P single bonds rather than as P₂, while nitrogen is happily diatomic.
∴ nitrogen.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|36||0|0.s:
An amphoteric oxide reacts with both acids and bases. Metal oxides go basic ⇒ amphoteric ⇒
acidic as you move right across a period and as the metal's electronegativity rises.
CaO, Na₂O and BaO are oxides of strongly electropositive s-block metals, so they are purely basic:
they dissolve in acid but not in alkali.
Al₂O₃ sits at the borderline and does both:
with acid — Al₂O₃ + 6HCl ⇒ 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O
with base — Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O ⇒ 2Na[Al(OH)₄]
That second reaction, dissolving in alkali as the aluminate, is the Bayer process used to purify
bauxite.
∴ Al₂O₃.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|37||0|0.s:
Check each equation against the chemistry it claims.
(A) MnO₂ + 4HCl ⇒ MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O — correct; this is the laboratory preparation of chlorine.
(B) 8NH₃ + 3Cl₂ ⇒ 6NH₄Cl + N₂ — correct; with *excess ammonia* chlorine oxidises some ammonia
to nitrogen and the HCl formed is taken up as ammonium chloride.
(D) 2Ca(OH)₂ + 2Cl₂ ⇒ Ca(OCl)₂ + CaCl₂ + 2H₂O — correct; this is how bleaching powder is made.
(C) 2NaOH + Cl₂ ⇒ 2NaCl + H₂ + O₂ — wrong. Chlorine disproportionates in cold dilute alkali;
it does not liberate hydrogen and oxygen. The real reaction is
Cl₂ + 2NaOH ⇒ NaCl + NaOCl + H₂O
Note the giveaway: producing H₂ and O₂ from NaOH would mean splitting water, which chlorine
cannot do.
∴ reaction (C) is the wrong one.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|38||0|0:
All noble gases are monatomic and unreactive, so what separates them here is size.
Atomic radius increases down the group: He < Ne < Ar < Kr.
Helium is the smallest atom of all, with just two electrons and a radius of about 31 pm.
Rubber, glass and many plastics are not fully dense at the atomic scale — they have gaps between
their polymer chains or in the silica network, and a helium atom is small enough to slip through them.
This is why helium balloons deflate within a day or two, and why helium is used to leak-test
vacuum systems: if there is a hole, helium will find it.
∴ helium.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|39||0|0.s:
The spin-only magnetic moment is μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM, so the largest μ belongs to the
configuration with the most unpaired electrons, n.
Fill the five d orbitals by Hund's rule — singly first, then pair up.
3d² : ↑ ↑ _ _ _ ⇒ n = 2, μ = √8 = 2.83 BM
3d⁵ : ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ ⇒ n = 5, μ = √35 = 5.92 BM ← maximum
3d⁷ : ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑ ↑ ↑ ⇒ n = 3, μ = √15 = 3.87 BM
3d⁸ : ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑ ↑ ⇒ n = 2, μ = √8 = 2.83 BM
d⁵ is the half-filled case: every orbital has one electron and none has had to pair, so it is the
most any 3d configuration can manage.
∴ 3d⁵.
